hypothetical_document.question: Why does ANCE select negatives from the whole corpus rather than relying only on local in-batch samples?
hypothetical_document.text: ANCE selects negatives from the entire corpus to ensure that the learned representations generalize effectively across diverse data distributions, whereas relying solely on local in-batch samples often leads to suboptimal contrastive learning due to limited diversity. By mining hard negatives globally, ANCE constructs a more robust loss landscape that forces the model to distinguish between semantically similar instances even when they appear far apart in the feature space. This global negative selection strategy significantly improves clustering performance on large-scale datasets like ImageNet-1K compared to methods restricted to batch-level supervision.

hypothetical_document.question: What result shows that Atlas can learn a knowledge-intensive task from very few examples?
hypothetical_document.text: In the study of few-shot learning capabilities, the Atlas model demonstrates its ability to master knowledge-intensive tasks with minimal data exposure. Specifically, when evaluated on complex reasoning benchmarks requiring extensive domain knowledge, Atlas achieved performance levels comparable to models trained on significantly larger datasets. This outcome highlights that Atlas does not merely rely on pattern matching but effectively internalizes abstract concepts through limited examples. Consequently, the experimental results confirm that Atlas can successfully transfer learned principles to novel tasks despite the scarcity of training instances provided during the initial phase.

Researchers have tested this collection using multiple retrieval models including BERT-based approaches, dense passage retrieval systems, and hybrid architectures that combine keyword matching with semantic similarity scoring.
